scenes.narration: The last chapter of Malcolm Fraser was written long after the fame. John Malcolm Fraser (; 21 May 1930 – 20 March 2015) was the 22nd prime minister of Australia, serving from 1975 to 1983. He held office as the leader of the Liberal Party of Australia, and is the fourth longest-serving prime minister in Australian history.

The whole life of Malcolm Fraser reads like a single decision repeated. Born in Melbourne, Fraser was raised on his father's sheep stations in rural New South Wales and studied philosophy, politics and economics at Magdalen College, Oxford. After an initial defeat in 1954, he was elected to the House of Representatives at the 1955 federal election, winning the rural south-western Victoria seat of Wannon.

Between the birth and the legend of Malcolm Fraser lie the years that actually decide it. At 25 years old, he was one of the youngest people ever elected to Parliament. When Harold Holt became prime minister in 1966, Fraser was appointed Minister for the Army.

The reputation of Malcolm Fraser was built in the middle, not at the edges. After Holt's disappearance and replacement by John Gorton, Fraser became Minister for Education and Science (1968–1969) and then Minister for Defence (1969–1971). In 1971, Fraser resigned from cabinet and denounced Gorton as "unfit to hold the great office of prime minister"; this precipitated the replacement of Gorton with William McMahon.

Somebody like Malcolm Fraser should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. After the Liberal–National Coalition was defeated at the 1972 election, Fraser unsuccessfully stood for the Liberal leadership, losing to Billy Snedden. When the party lost the 1974 election, he began to move against Snedden, eventually mounting a successful challenge in March 1975.

The life of Malcolm Fraser begins far from where the story usually starts. As Leader of the Opposition, Fraser used the Coalition's control of the Australian Senate to block supply to the Whitlam government, precipitating the 1975 Australian constitutional crisis. This culminated with Gough Whitlam being dismissed as prime minister by the governor-general, Sir John Kerr, a unique occurrence in Australian history.

Malcolm Fraser was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. The correctness of Fraser's actions in the crisis and the exact nature of his involvement in Kerr's decision have since been a topic of debate. Fraser remains the only Australian prime minister to ascend to the position upon the dismissal of his predecessor.

To understand where Malcolm Fraser ended up, start with where Malcolm Fraser began. After Whitlam's dismissal, Fraser was sworn in as prime minister on an initial caretaker basis. The Coalition won a landslide victory at the 1975 election, and was re-elected in 1977 and 1980.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Malcolm Fraser ran through years nobody filmed. Fraser took a keen interest in foreign affairs as prime minister, and was more active in the international sphere than many of his predecessors. He was a strong supporter of multiculturalism, and during his term in office Australia admitted significant numbers of non-white immigrants (including Vietnamese boat people) for the first time, effectively ending the White Australia policy.

Each stage of the life of Malcolm Fraser made the next stage possible. Particularly in his final years in office, Fraser came into conflict with the "dry" economic rationalist and fiscal conservative faction of his party. In his post-political career, he held advisory positions with the United Nations (UN) and the Commonwealth of Nations, and was president of the aid agency CARE from 1990 to 1995.

The people who knew Malcolm Fraser young describe someone already restless. He resigned his membership of the Liberal Party in 2009 after the election of Tony Abbott as leader, Fraser having been a critic of the Liberals’ policy direction for a number of years. He was the last Australian prime minister entitled to the style "the Right Honourable" as a member of the Privy Council of the United Kingdom.

What Malcolm Fraser built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. His seven and a half-year tenure as prime minister is the fourth-longest in Australian history, only surpassed by Bob Hawke, John Howard and Robert Menzies. John Malcolm Fraser was born in Toorak, Melbourne, Victoria, on 21 May 1930.

By the time Malcolm Fraser reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. He was the second of two children born to Una Arnold (née Woolf) and John Neville Fraser; his older sister Lorraine had been born in 1928. Both he and his father were known exclusively by their middle names.

The rise of Malcolm Fraser was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. His paternal grandfather, Sir Simon Fraser, was born in Nova Scotia, Canada, and arrived in Australia in 1853. He made his fortune as a railway contractor, and later acquired significant pastoral holdings, becoming a member of the "squattocracy".

Setbacks came early for Malcolm Fraser, and the response to them is the real story. Fraser's maternal grandfather, Louis Woolf, was born in Dunedin, New Zealand, and arrived in Australia as a child. He was of Jewish origin, a fact which his grandson did not learn until he was an adult.

The legacy of Malcolm Fraser outlived the circumstances that produced it. A chartered accountant by trade, he married Amy Booth, who was related to the wealthy Hordern family of Sydney and was a first cousin of Sir Samuel Hordern. His father served on the Wakool Shire Council, including as president for two years, and was an admirer of Billy Hughes and a friend of Richard Casey.

Few lives travel as far as that of Malcolm Fraser, and the distance is the point. Simon Fraser served in both houses of the colonial Parliament of Victoria, and represented Victoria at several of the constitutional conventions of the 1890s. He eventually become one of the inaugural members of the new federal Senate, serving from 1901 to 1913 as a member of the early conservative parties.

The childhood of Malcolm Fraser contains the adult in small print. Louis Woolf also stood for the Senate in 1901, standing as a Free Trader in Western Australia. He polled only 400 votes across the whole state, and was never again a candidate for public office.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Malcolm Fraser — in that order. Fraser spent most of his early life at Balpool-Nyang, a sheep station of 15,000 hectares (37,000 acres) on the Edward River near Moulamein, New South Wales. His father had a law degree from Magdalen College, Oxford, but never practised law and preferred the life of a grazier.

The turning point in the life of Malcolm Fraser looked like a failure at the time. Fraser contracted a severe case of pneumonia when he was eight years old, which nearly proved fatal. He was home-schooled until the age of ten, when he was sent to board at Tudor House School in the Southern Highlands.

Every biography of Malcolm Fraser has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. He attended Tudor House from 1940 to 1943, and then completed his secondary education at Melbourne Grammar School from 1944 to 1948 where he was a member of Rusden House. While at Melbourne Grammar, he lived in a flat that his parents owned on Collins Street.

The education of Malcolm Fraser happened mostly outside any school. In 1943, Fraser's father sold Balpool-Nyang – which had been prone to drought – and bought Nareen, in the Western District of Victoria. He was devastated by the sale of his childhood home, and regarded the day he found out about it as the worst of his life.

What Malcolm Fraser wanted at the start and what Malcolm Fraser got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. In 1949, Fraser moved to England to study at Magdalen College, Oxford, which his father had also attended. Although Fraser did not excel academically, he regarded his time at Oxford as his intellectual awakening, where he learned "how to think".

The defining trait of Malcolm Fraser was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. In his second year, he had a relationship with Anne Reid, who as Anne Fairbairn later became a prominent poet. After graduating, Fraser considered taking a law degree or joining the British Army, but eventually decided to return to Australia and take over the running of the family property.

Those who met Malcolm Fraser at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. He began attending meetings of the Young Liberals in Hamilton, and became acquainted with many of the local party officials. In November 1953, aged 23, Fraser unexpectedly won Liberal preselection for the Division of Wannon, which covered most of Victoria's Western District.

The private years of Malcolm Fraser explain the public decades better than any speech. The previous Liberal member, Dan Mackinnon, had been defeated in 1951 and moved to a different electorate. He was expected to be succeeded by Magnus Cormack, who had recently lost his place in the Senate.

The family Malcolm Fraser came from matters more than the legends admit. Fraser had put his name forward as a way of building a profile for future candidacies, but mounted a strong campaign and in the end won a narrow victory. In January 1954, he made the first of a series of weekly radio broadcasts on 3HA Hamilton and 3YB Warrnambool, titled One Australia.

The first real success of Malcolm Fraser arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. His program – consisting of a pre-recorded 15-minute monologue – covered a wide range of topics, and was often reprinted in newspapers. It continued more or less uninterrupted until his retirement from politics in 1983, and helped him build a substantial personal following in his electorate.

The last chapter of Malcolm Fraser was written long after the fame. At the 1954 election, Fraser lost to the sitting Labor member Don McLeod by just 17 votes (out of over 37,000 cast). However, he reprised his candidacy at the early 1955 election after a redistribution made Wannon notionally Liberal.

The whole life of Malcolm Fraser reads like a single decision repeated. These factors, combined with the 1955 Labor Party split, allowed Fraser to win a landslide victory. Fraser took his seat in parliament at the age of 25 – the youngest sitting MP by four years, and the first who had been too young to serve in World War II.

Between the birth and the legend of Malcolm Fraser lie the years that actually decide it. He was re-elected at the 1958 election despite being restricted in his campaigning by a bout of hepatitis. Fraser was soon being touted as a future member of cabinet, but despite good relations with Robert Menzies never served in cabinet during Menzies' tenure.

The reputation of Malcolm Fraser was built in the middle, not at the edges. His long wait for ministerial preferment was probably due to a combination of his youth and the fact that Menzies' ministries already contained a disproportionately high number of Victorians. Fraser spoke on a wide range of topics during his early years in parliament, but took a particular interest in foreign affairs.

Somebody like Malcolm Fraser should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. In 1964, he and Gough Whitlam were both awarded Leader Grants by the United States Department of State, allowing them to spend two months in Washington, D.C., getting to know American political and military leaders. The Vietnam War was the main topic of conversation, and on his return trip to Australia he spent two days in Saigon.
